energia.title: Energy
text:
In every electricity supply, two key concepts must be distinguished: POWER and ENERGY.
This will help us better understand what each concept represents within the electricity bill.
CONTRACTED POWER (CP)
What is it?
It is the fixed term on the bill.
In supplies above 15 kW, the contracted power is three-phase.
It represents the maximum electrical power capacity that can be requested at a given moment.
In other words: the amount of machinery that can operate simultaneously.
It mainly affects installations with 3.0TD and 6.1TD access tariffs:
— 3.0TD: power levels above 15 kW.
— 6.1TD: power levels above 450 kW.
In a three-phase system, the total power (kW) is divided among the three phases.
This allows higher electrical loads to be managed.
It is essential for industries, large companies, or homes with equipment such as elevators,
swimming pools, or garage doors.
CONSUMED ENERGY (CE)
What is it?
It is the variable term on the bill.
It represents the cost of the electricity actually consumed during the billing period.
It depends on how long the devices are operating.
It is calculated by multiplying the kWh consumed by the tariff's kWh price.
MAIN FEATURES
Load distribution:
Power is distributed across the three phases.
With digital meters, this distribution may be uneven depending on the needs.
Time periods and seasons:
Since June 2021 there have been 6 power periods (P1–P6) and 4 energy seasons.
The periods and seasons depend on the month and the tariff type.
Common voltages:
— Medium voltage (MV): 380–400 V.
— High voltage (HV): 1 kV to 30 kV.
It depends on the type of business.

calendari.title: Calendar
text:
TIME PERIODS AND SEASONS
Supplies above 15 kW (3.0TD, 6.1TD, MV and HV) use a billing structure
based on 6 time periods and 4 energy seasons.
Power is billed across the 6 periods regardless of the season, while energy
is billed according to the season in which it is consumed. This was the main regulatory change
included in CNMC Circular 3/2020 of January 15 and came into force in June 2021.
TIME PERIODS (P1 TO P6)
Each period has a different price and specific application hours.
— P1: High season. Months: December, January, February, and July.
— P2: High and medium-high seasons. In addition to the previous months, March and November.
— P3: Medium-high and medium seasons. March, November, June, August, and September.
— P4: Medium and low seasons. June, August, September, April, May, and October.
— P5: Low season: April, May, and October.
— P6: Common throughout the year.
For example, in December P1, P2, and P6 are billed. In March, P2, P3, and P6 are billed.
In June we have P3, P4, and P6. And in September P4, P5, and P6. The P6 period is common throughout the year.
And in some electricity retailers it is common to call them peak, flat, or valley instead of P1, P2, and P6.
PERIOD HOURS (PENINSULAR TIME)
P1: 08:00 to 09:00, from 14:00 to 18:00, and from 22:00 to 00:00.
P2: 08:00 to 09:00, from 14:00 to 18:00, and from 22:00 to 00:00.
P3: 08:00 to 09:00, from 14:00 to 18:00, and from 22:00 to 00:00.
P4: 08:00 to 09:00, from 14:00 to 18:00, and from 22:00 to 00:00.
P5: 08:00 to 09:00, from 14:00 to 18:00, and from 22:00 to 00:00.
P6: Weekends and public holidays (all day).
ENERGY SEASONS (CONSUMED ENERGY)
The season determines the price applied to periods P1 to P6.
There are 4 seasons: high, medium-high, medium, and low.
MONTHS BY SEASON
High season: January, February, July, December.
Medium-high season: March, June, October.
Medium season: April, May, November.
Low season: August, September.
HOW IS THIS APPLIED?
In 3.0TD and 6.1TD tariffs, periods P1 to P6 are applied equally, but with specific prices.
The P6 period is especially relevant in MV and HV due to its reduced tariff.
Companies can optimize costs by shifting consumption to P5 and P6.
SUMMARY
CP: 6 fixed periods each month.
Energy: or consumption. 4 seasons that vary depending on the month.
Each period has specific hours and a different price.

reactiva.title: Reactive
text:
REACTIVE ENERGY
Reactive energy is an “indirect” electrical consumption generated mainly by motors and
industrial equipment.
It does not perform useful work, but it overloads the installation and usually generates surcharges on the bill.
It is reduced with compensation equipment such as CAPACITOR BANKS, which act like an entry-only gate, allowing the necessary current to enter
but only using what the machine needs at that moment, while the rest is used by the installation.
In other words, when a machine starts up it generates a voltage peak, but does not use all of it
and sends part of it back to the grid, which is what is called 'gross energy'. Since it cannot be used, it is penalized
because that energy is lost. Some examples are freezers, elevators, cold storage rooms, etc.
PHOTOVOLTAICS AND SURPLUS COMPENSATION:
Photovoltaic panels are what generate these surpluses:
There are times when we do not consume all the energy produced by our installation, such as during holidays.
or during a season of lower production, our PV system will continue producing for self-consumption, but part of that production will not be consumed.
In this situation, our PV system generates surpluses.
And surpluses are the energy PRODUCED BUT NOT CONSUMED that is returned to the grid
and compensated according to electricity market conditions with regulated limitations.
Photovoltaic installations are usually sized mainly to cover
their own consumption, and oversizing them solely to generate surpluses is generally not very profitable
and is subject to technical and regulatory limitations, such as connection point capacity.

tarifa.title: Access tariffs
text:
ACCESS TARIFFS FOR BUSINESSES
Businesses mainly work with two access tariffs: 2.0TD and 3.0TD.
Your choice depends on your contracted power.
TARIFF 2.0TD
For businesses with contracted power up to 15 kW.
Has 3 time periods: Peak (P1), Flat (P2) and Valley (P3).
— Peak: hours of maximum demand (highest price).
— Flat: intermediate hours.
— Valley: nights and weekends (lowest price).
Ideal for small shops, bars, offices and premises.
TARIFF 3.0TD
For businesses with contracted power above 15 kW.
Has 6 time periods (P1 to P6) and 4 energy seasons.
Allows greater optimisation of consumption by time slot.
Common in supermarkets, restaurants, hotels and medium-sized businesses.
HOW DOES IT AFFECT YOUR BILL?
The power charge is fixed and paid for contracted power in each period.
The energy charge is variable and depends on actual consumption in each time slot.
Consuming in off-peak hours can significantly reduce your bill.

calendari.title: Periods and schedules
text:
TIME PERIODS FOR BUSINESSES
The time period system determines when energy is more or less expensive.
TARIFF 2.0TD — 3 PERIODS
— P1 (Peak): Monday to Friday from 10:00 to 14:00 and from 18:00 to 22:00.
— P2 (Flat): Monday to Friday from 08:00 to 10:00, 14:00 to 18:00 and 22:00 to 00:00.
— P3 (Valley): from 00:00 to 08:00, weekends and national holidays.
TARIFF 3.0TD — 6 PERIODS
Works like industry: 6 periods (P1 to P6) with 4 annual seasons.
— High season: January, February, July, December.
— Medium-high season: March, June, October.
— Medium season: April, May, November.
— Low season: August, September.
PRACTICAL TIP
If your business has more than 15 kW, check the detailed schedule in the industry section.

factura.title: Reading your invoice
text:
HOW TO READ A BUSINESS ELECTRICITY INVOICE
A business electricity invoice has two main blocks: fixed and variable charges.
POWER CHARGE (FIXED)
What you pay for having electricity connected, regardless of consumption.
Depends on the contracted power in each period.
If you have contracted more power than you need, you are overpaying.
If you exceed contracted power, a surcharge for excess power applies.
ENERGY CHARGE (VARIABLE)
What you pay for actual consumption in kWh.
The price varies by time period (P1 is the most expensive, P3 or P6 the cheapest).
OTHER ITEMS
Taxes: VAT (21%) and electricity tax (5.11%).
Meter rental: Cost of the meter and measuring equipment.
SAVINGS OPPORTUNITIES
Check whether contracted power matches actual consumption needs.
Identify avoidable high consumption during peak hours.
Compare supplier offers under the same network conditions.

llar.heroSubtitle: We help you understand your bill and reduce consumption without changing your habits.
llar.introTitle: What you need to know about your supply
llar.introLead: Home energy supply is the most common but also the least understood. Knowing how it works lets you make decisions and save without effort.
introItems: Tariff: Homes are always on the 2.0TD tariff, the only residential tariff.
Contracted power: The maximum simultaneous consumption capacity. Most homes work between 3.45 kW and 10 kW, although higher powers can exist.
Energy periods: The 2.0TD has 3 time periods with schedules fixed by regulation. The price of each hour is determined by OMIE, the Iberian electricity market operator.
Time-of-use pricing: Since June 2021, all residential supplies have automatic time-of-use pricing. It is not optional — everyone pays differently in peak, flat and valley hours.
Self-consumption: Can be individual or collective (communities of owners). Surplus compensation depends on the type of installation and the contract conditions.

tarifa.title: Tariff 2.0TD
text:
THE 2.0TD TARIFF — THE RESIDENTIAL TARIFF
All homes in Spain are on the 2.0TD access tariff.
It is the only residential tariff available since the regulatory reform of June 2021.
WHAT THE 2.0TD INCLUDES
It has 3 time periods: Peak (P1), Flat (P2) and Valley (P3).
The schedules for each period are fixed by regulation and are the same for everyone.
— P1 (Peak): Monday to Friday from 10:00 to 14:00 and from 18:00 to 22:00.
— P2 (Flat): Monday to Friday from 08:00 to 10:00, from 14:00 to 18:00 and from 22:00 to 00:00.
— P3 (Valley): from 00:00 to 08:00, weekends and national holidays.
HOW THE PRICE IS DETERMINED
The price of energy in each period is set by OMIE (Iberian Energy Market Operator).
If you are on PVPC (voluntary price for small consumers), your price varies every hour with the market.
If you have a fixed tariff with a supplier, the price is agreed in the contract.
POWER CHARGE
Most homes work between 3.45 kW and 10 kW.
It is important to have the power correctly set for 2 reasons: 1- If we demand more, the meter cuts the supply, and 2- If we have too much, we overpay.
Check whether the contracted power is adequate to avoid overpaying or supply micro-cuts.

discriminacio.title: Periods and schedules
text:
TIME PERIODS FOR HOMES
Since June 2021, all residential supplies have automatic time-of-use pricing.
It is not an option that can be activated or deactivated: it is part of the 2.0TD tariff for everyone.
WHAT THIS MEANS IN PRACTICE
The price of energy varies depending on the period in which it is consumed.
— P1 (Peak): the most expensive. Monday to Friday from 10:00 to 14:00 and from 18:00 to 22:00.
— P2 (Flat): intermediate price. Monday to Friday during the remaining working hours.
— P3 (Valley): the cheapest. Nights, weekends and national holidays.
HOW TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF PRICES
Shifting intensive consumption (washing machine, dishwasher, electric vehicle charging)
to off-peak hours can generate real and sustained savings on the bill.
It is not necessary to radically change habits: small schedule adjustments have an impact.
THE PRICE IS SET BY THE MARKET
For PVPC, the exact price of each hour is published daily by OMIE.
For fixed tariffs, the price per period is agreed with the supplier.

autoconsum.title: Self-consumption
text:
SELF-CONSUMPTION IN HOMES
Self-consumption allows generating your own energy, mainly through solar panels,
and thus reducing the energy purchased from the grid.
TYPES OF SELF-CONSUMPTION
— Individual: own installation in a detached house or flat with available rooftop space.
— Collective: several homes in a community of owners share a common installation.
The collective model allows distributing generation among participants according to agreed coefficients.
SURPLUS COMPENSATION
When more energy is generated than consumed, the surplus can be returned to the grid.
The financial compensation for these surpluses depends on:
— The type of self-consumption contract signed.
— The conditions agreed with the supplier.
— The market price at the time of injection.
IMPORTANT CONSIDERATIONS
Oversizing the installation just to generate surpluses is usually not very profitable.
The optimal sizing aims to cover own consumption, not to maximise sales to the grid.
There are technical and regulatory limitations at connection points that affect the project.
Each case requires a specific analysis before making investment decisions.
